q: Which drug contains an ester linkage and is metabolised by plasma cholinesterase?
why: Ester local anaesthetics (cocaine, procaine, chloroprocaine, tetracaine) are hydrolysed by plasma esterases, producing para-aminobenzoic acid, which can cause allergy. Amides (with an 'i' before '-caine') are metabolised in the liver.

q: Which drug is a quaternary ammonium compound and therefore does not readily cross the blood–brain barrier?
why: Glycopyrronium is a quaternary amine, permanently charged, so it does not cross the blood–brain barrier or placenta significantly. Atropine and hyoscine are tertiary amines and can cause central effects (central anticholinergic syndrome).

q: Lidocaine (pKa 7.9) is injected into infected, acidic tissue. Why is its effect reduced?
o: More drug is ionised and cannot cross the membrane
The drug becomes more protein bound
why: In acidic tissue, a weak base becomes more ionised (pH below pKa), so less unionised drug crosses the lipid membrane to reach its intracellular site of action. The ionised form is what blocks the sodium channel from inside.

q: Which drug is marketed as a single enantiomer (an S-isomer) to reduce cardiotoxicity?
why: Levobupivacaine is the S-enantiomer of bupivacaine, and ropivacaine is also an S-enantiomer; both are less cardiotoxic. Esketamine is the S-enantiomer of ketamine, more potent with fewer psychotomimetic effects. Atracurium is a mixture of 10 stereoisomers; cisatracurium is one of them.

q: Which receptor is a ligand-gated ion channel?
why: Ligand-gated ion channels include nicotinic, GABA-A, 5-HT3, NMDA and glycine receptors. Muscarinic, adrenergic and opioid receptors are G protein-coupled receptors. Insulin acts via a tyrosine kinase receptor; steroids act via intracellular receptors.

q: Which G protein is coupled to the beta-1 adrenoceptor?
why: Beta receptors couple to Gs (adenylyl cyclase, cAMP rise). Alpha-2, M2 and opioid receptors couple to Gi; alpha-1, M1 and M3 receptors couple to Gq (phospholipase C, IP3, DAG, calcium release).

q: A drug has high affinity for a receptor but an intrinsic activity of zero. How is it classified?
why: An antagonist binds (affinity) but produces no response (efficacy 0). A partial agonist has intrinsic activity between 0 and 1; an inverse agonist produces the opposite effect to an agonist (negative efficacy).

q: How does a competitive antagonist affect the agonist log dose–response curve?
o: Parallel shift to the right, same maximum
why: A reversible competitive antagonist causes a parallel rightward shift; increasing agonist dose overcomes it. A non-competitive (or irreversible) antagonist reduces the maximum response. The pA2 quantifies competitive antagonist potency.

q: Which drug is a potent enzyme inducer of cytochrome P450 enzymes?
why: Inducers include rifampicin, carbamazepine, phenytoin, phenobarbital, St John's wort and chronic alcohol. Inhibitors include macrolides, azole antifungals, amiodarone, cimetidine, omeprazole, ritonavir and grapefruit juice.

q: Why can clarithromycin cause excessive sedation in a patient taking midazolam?
o: It inhibits CYP3A4, reducing midazolam metabolism
why: Midazolam is metabolised by CYP3A4. Inhibitors (macrolides, azoles, HIV protease inhibitors, diltiazem) increase its plasma levels and prolong sedation. Inducers reduce its effect.

q: Which enzyme is inhibited by NSAIDs?
why: NSAIDs inhibit COX-1 and COX-2, reducing prostaglandin and thromboxane synthesis. Corticosteroids indirectly inhibit phospholipase A2. Leukotrienes come from the lipoxygenase pathway, which is relevant to aspirin-exacerbated respiratory disease.

q: Why does aspirin produce a long-lasting antiplatelet effect?
why: Platelets lack nuclei, so irreversible COX-1 acetylation lasts the platelet's lifespan (7–10 days). Low doses selectively reduce thromboxane A2 while sparing endothelial prostacyclin.

q: According to Rawlins and Thompson, a predictable, dose-related adverse drug reaction is classified as which type?
why: Type A (augmented) reactions are dose-related and predictable (e.g. respiratory depression with opioids). Type B (bizarre) are unpredictable (e.g. anaphylaxis, malignant hyperthermia). C: chronic; D: delayed; E: end-of-use; F: failure of therapy.

q: Which is an example of a pharmaceutical (in vitro) drug interaction?
o: Thiopental precipitating in a line with rocuronium
why: Pharmaceutical interactions occur outside the body, e.g. thiopental (alkaline) precipitating with acidic drugs. Pharmacokinetic interactions affect ADME; pharmacodynamic interactions occur at the site of action (synergy or antagonism).

q: Anaphylaxis to a neuromuscular blocking drug is which type of hypersensitivity reaction?
why: Type I is immediate and IgE-mediated, with mast cell degranulation. Type II is antibody against cell surface antigens (e.g. ABO incompatibility, HIT). Type III is immune complex (serum sickness); type IV is delayed T cell (contact dermatitis).

q: Heparin-induced thrombocytopenia (type II) is mediated by which mechanism?
why: HIT antibodies (IgG) bind PF4–heparin complexes and activate platelets via FcγRIIa, causing thrombocytopenia and thrombosis, typically 5–10 days after starting heparin. Stop heparin and give a non-heparin anticoagulant (e.g. argatroban).

q: Which route of administration avoids hepatic first-pass metabolism?
why: Sublingual, buccal, transdermal, inhaled, intranasal and parenteral routes avoid first-pass metabolism. The lower rectum drains partly into systemic veins, but the upper rectum drains via the portal system.

q: Oral bioavailability is defined as which ratio?
o: Peak oral concentration / peak IV concentration
why: Bioavailability (F) = (AUC oral × IV dose)/(AUC IV × oral dose). It is reduced by poor absorption and first-pass metabolism (gut wall and liver).

q: Which factor speeds the rise of alveolar concentration (FA/FI) of a volatile agent?
why: FA/FI rises faster with increased ventilation, higher inspired concentration (concentration effect), low blood:gas solubility and low cardiac output. A high cardiac output removes more agent from the alveoli, slowing the rise.

q: What is the second gas effect?
o: Two gases cancel out each other's effects
Rapid N2O uptake concentrates the second gas
A volatile increases N2O solubility in blood
Diffusion hypoxia at the end of anaesthesia
The second agent increases N2O metabolism
why: Rapid uptake of a large volume of N2O concentrates the remaining alveolar gases (including the volatile and O2) and draws more gas into the lungs, accelerating uptake of the second agent. Diffusion hypoxia (Fink effect) occurs at the end when N2O leaves the blood.

q: Which cytochrome P450 isoenzyme metabolises the largest proportion of drugs?
why: CYP3A4 metabolises about half of drugs, including midazolam, fentanyl, alfentanil, lidocaine and many others. CYP2D6 converts codeine and tramadol to more active metabolites; CYP2E1 metabolises sevoflurane and paracetamol (to NAPQI).

q: A patient who is a CYP2D6 ultra-rapid metaboliser is given codeine. What is the risk?
why: Codeine is a prodrug converted to morphine by CYP2D6. Ultra-rapid metabolisers produce excess morphine, risking toxicity (deaths in children after tonsillectomy). Poor metabolisers (about 8% of Europeans) get little analgesia.

q: In a three-compartment model of propofol, what does the rapid initial fall in plasma concentration after a bolus mainly represent?
why: The early fall reflects redistribution to the fast compartment (vessel-rich tissues and muscle), explaining offset after a single bolus. Later phases reflect slower redistribution (fat) and elimination.

q: What does context-sensitive half-time describe?
o: Elimination half-life after a single bolus
Time from bolus to peak effect
Half-life of the main active metabolite
Time for a 50% fall after stopping an infusion
why: Context-sensitive half-time depends on infusion duration. Remifentanil's is about 3–4 minutes regardless of duration (esterase metabolism); fentanyl's rises markedly with longer infusions because of large peripheral compartments.

q: A drug has a clearance of 1 L/min and a volume of distribution of 70 L. What is its elimination half-life?
Which drug property tends to produce a large volume of distribution?
o: High lipid solubility and tissue binding
why: Lipid-soluble drugs with extensive tissue binding (e.g. fentanyl, amiodarone) have large Vd. Highly protein-bound, ionised or large molecules (e.g. warfarin, neuromuscular blockers, heparin) have small Vd, close to plasma or ECF volume.

sb: Drug Metabolism - Phase I & II Reactions
q: Which reaction is a phase II metabolic reaction?
why: Phase I reactions (oxidation, reduction, hydrolysis) introduce or expose functional groups. Phase II reactions are conjugations (glucuronidation, sulphation, acetylation, methylation, glutathione conjugation), producing water-soluble metabolites.

sb: Drug Metabolism - Phase I & II Reactions
q: Morphine is metabolised mainly to morphine-6-glucuronide. What is the clinical significance?
o: It is inactive at opioid receptors
It is converted back to codeine
It is excreted only in bile
It is active and accumulates in renal failure
why: M6G is a more potent mu agonist than morphine and accumulates in renal impairment, causing prolonged sedation and respiratory depression. M3G (the main metabolite) is inactive at opioid receptors but may cause neuroexcitation.

q: Which drug undergoes significant enterohepatic recirculation?
why: Drugs excreted in bile as conjugates and then deconjugated by gut bacteria are reabsorbed (e.g. mycophenolate, oestrogens, morphine to a degree, rifampicin). Antibiotics can disrupt this, reducing oral contraceptive efficacy (now considered a minor effect).

q: How is aspirin overdose excretion enhanced?
o: Alkalinising the urine with sodium bicarbonate
why: Salicylate is a weak acid; urinary alkalinisation increases ionisation in the tubule, trapping it in the urine (ion trapping). Haemodialysis is used in severe poisoning.

q: In propofol target-controlled infusion, which model targets the effect-site concentration?
why: The Schnider model is commonly used in effect-site mode and adjusts for age, weight, height and sex. The Marsh model is typically plasma-targeted and uses weight only. Minto is used for remifentanil; Paedfusor and Kataria are paediatric propofol models. Eleveld is a newer general-purpose propofol model.

q: What is ke0 in a target-controlled infusion model?
o: The infusion rate at steady state
The rate constant for equilibration between plasma and effect site
The clearance from the fat compartment
The elimination rate constant from the central compartment
why: ke0 describes how quickly the effect site equilibrates with plasma. A larger ke0 means faster equilibration (shorter t½ke0). Effect-site targeting overshoots plasma concentration to reach the target faster.

q: Why are neonates more sensitive to non-depolarising neuromuscular blockers?
o: Immature junctions with fewer acetylcholine receptors
why: Neonates are more sensitive at the receptor level, but their larger ECF volume increases Vd, so initial doses per kg are similar. Clearance is reduced, so duration may be longer. Neonates are relatively resistant to suxamethonium (needs about 2 mg/kg).

q: How does pregnancy affect the minimum alveolar concentration of volatile agents?
why: MAC falls by up to about 30% in pregnancy, possibly from progesterone and endorphins. Increased minute ventilation and reduced FRC also speed inhalational induction.

q: What is MAC?
o: Maximum alveolar concentration that is safe
Alveolar concentration preventing movement to incision in 50%
why: MAC is the minimum alveolar concentration at steady state (1 atm) that prevents movement in response to a standard surgical incision in 50% of subjects. MAC-awake is about 0.3–0.5 MAC. MAC is lowered by age, hypothermia, pregnancy and opioids.

q: Approximately what is the MAC of sevoflurane in a 40-year-old adult?
why: MAC (age about 40): halothane 0.75%, isoflurane 1.17%, sevoflurane about 2%, desflurane about 6%, N2O about 104%. MAC falls about 6% per decade after 40.

q: Which induction agent is an NMDA receptor antagonist and preserves airway reflexes and blood pressure better than others?
why: Ketamine causes dissociative anaesthesia, sympathomimetic effects (BP and HR increase, except in catecholamine depletion), bronchodilation and relative preservation of airway reflexes and respiratory drive. It increases secretions and can cause emergence phenomena.

q: Which induction agent causes adrenocortical suppression by inhibiting 11-beta-hydroxylase?
why: Etomidate inhibits 11-beta-hydroxylase, suppressing cortisol synthesis for 6–24 h after a single dose, a concern in sepsis. It is cardiovascularly stable but causes myoclonus and PONV.

q: Why does suxamethonium cause hyperkalaemia in burns patients after about 24–48 hours?
why: Denervation, burns, immobility and crush injury lead to proliferation of extrajunctional receptors (including fetal γ and α7 types). Depolarisation releases large amounts of potassium. Avoid suxamethonium from about 24–48 h until recovery.

q: What is the recommended dose of sugammadex to reverse a profound rocuronium block (post-tetanic count 1–2)?
why: Sugammadex: 2 mg/kg if TOF count is 2 or more; 4 mg/kg if PTC is 1–2; 16 mg/kg for immediate reversal after 1.2 mg/kg rocuronium. It encapsulates rocuronium and vecuronium, not benzylisoquinoliniums.

q: What is the maximum recommended dose of plain bupivacaine?
why: Commonly quoted maxima: bupivacaine and levobupivacaine 2 mg/kg (adrenaline does not substantially change this), lidocaine 3 mg/kg plain or 7 mg/kg with adrenaline, prilocaine 6 mg/kg plain (8 mg/kg with felypressin), ropivacaine 3 mg/kg. Site of injection affects peak levels.

q: Which local anaesthetic is associated with methaemoglobinaemia at high doses?
why: Prilocaine is metabolised to o-toluidine, which oxidises haemoglobin to methaemoglobin, usually above about 600 mg in adults. Benzocaine also causes it. Treatment is methylene blue 1–2 mg/kg.

q: What is the toxic metabolite of paracetamol in overdose?
why: In overdose, glucuronidation and sulphation saturate and more drug is oxidised by CYP2E1 and 3A4 to NAPQI. Once glutathione is depleted, NAPQI causes centrilobular hepatic necrosis. Acetylcysteine replenishes glutathione.

q: Which NSAID is a selective COX-2 inhibitor?
why: Coxibs (parecoxib, celecoxib, etoricoxib) selectively inhibit COX-2, causing less gastric toxicity and no platelet inhibition, but they still have renal effects and an increased cardiovascular thrombotic risk.

q: Which opioid is metabolised by non-specific plasma and tissue esterases?
why: Remifentanil's ester linkage is hydrolysed by non-specific esterases, giving a context-sensitive half-time of about 3–4 min and no accumulation, even in hepatic or renal failure. It is not metabolised by plasma cholinesterase.

q: Why does alfentanil have a faster onset than fentanyl despite lower lipid solubility?
o: It has a larger volume of distribution
Its low pKa leaves about 90% unionised
It is given in higher doses
Its pKa is higher than fentanyl's
why: Alfentanil's low pKa (6.5) means about 90% is unionised at pH 7.4 (fentanyl, pKa 8.4, is about 9% unionised), so it crosses the blood–brain barrier quickly. Its small Vd also gives high concentration gradients.

q: Which drug increases cardiac contractility by inhibiting phosphodiesterase III?
why: Milrinone (PDE3 inhibitor) increases cAMP, giving inotropy and vasodilatation (inodilator). Dobutamine is a beta-1 agonist; levosimendan is a calcium sensitiser; digoxin inhibits Na⁺/K⁺ ATPase.

q: Which antiarrhythmic drug is a Vaughan Williams class III agent?
why: Class I: sodium channel blockers (Ia procainamide, Ib lidocaine, Ic flecainide). II: beta-blockers. III: potassium channel blockers (amiodarone, sotalol), prolonging repolarisation. IV: calcium channel blockers (verapamil, diltiazem).

q: Which bronchodilator acts by blocking muscarinic M3 receptors?
why: Ipratropium and tiotropium are muscarinic antagonists. Salbutamol is a beta-2 agonist; aminophylline is a phosphodiesterase inhibitor and adenosine antagonist; montelukast blocks leukotriene receptors.

q: What is the therapeutic range of plasma theophylline?
why: Theophylline has a narrow therapeutic range (10–20 mg/L, some use 5–15). Toxicity causes nausea, arrhythmias and seizures. Levels rise with enzyme inhibitors (e.g. erythromycin, ciprofloxacin) and fall with smoking.

q: How does metoclopramide work as an antiemetic and prokinetic?
why: Metoclopramide blocks D2 receptors in the CTZ and enhances upper GI motility via 5-HT4 agonism and cholinergic effects. It can cause extrapyramidal effects and is avoided in bowel obstruction and Parkinson's disease.

q: Which drug irreversibly inhibits the gastric H⁺/K⁺ ATPase?
why: Proton pump inhibitors are prodrugs activated in acid to irreversibly inhibit the proton pump. H2 antagonists (ranitidine, famotidine) block histamine at parietal cells. Sodium citrate neutralises existing acid.

q: Where do thiazide diuretics act?
why: Thiazides block the NCC in the DCT, causing hypokalaemia, hyponatraemia, hypercalcaemia (reduced calcium excretion), hyperglycaemia and hyperuricaemia. Loop diuretics block NKCC2; amiloride blocks ENaC; spironolactone blocks aldosterone receptors.

q: Mannitol reduces intracranial pressure mainly by which mechanism?
o: Osmotic shift of water out of the brain
why: Mannitol (0.25–1 g/kg) raises plasma osmolality, drawing water from brain tissue. It also reduces blood viscosity, causing reflex vasoconstriction. It is an osmotic diuretic; monitor osmolality (keep under about 320 mOsm/kg).

q: Which drug is first-line in the UK for preventing postpartum haemorrhage at caesarean section?
why: Oxytocin (e.g. a slow 3–5 IU bolus or infusion) is first-line. Carbetocin is an alternative. Ergometrine is avoided in hypertension and pre-eclampsia. Carboprost (PGF2α) is avoided in asthma.

q: Which drug is a tocolytic used to relax the uterus?
why: Tocolytics include beta-2 agonists (terbutaline), nifedipine, atosiban (oxytocin receptor antagonist) and GTN for acute relaxation. Oxytocin, ergometrine and prostaglandins are uterotonics.

q: Which antiepileptic drug acts mainly by blocking voltage-gated sodium channels?
why: Carbamazepine, phenytoin and lamotrigine block sodium channels. Levetiracetam binds SV2A; gabapentin binds the α2δ subunit of calcium channels; ethosuximide blocks T-type calcium channels; benzodiazepines enhance GABA-A.

q: A patient on an MAOI needs a vasopressor. Which drug is most likely to cause a dangerous hypertensive response?
why: Indirect-acting sympathomimetics (ephedrine) release stored noradrenaline, which accumulates with MAO inhibition, causing hypertensive crises. Direct-acting agents in small titrated doses are preferred. Pethidine and tramadol risk serotonin toxicity.

q: Which drug increases insulin secretion by closing ATP-sensitive potassium channels on beta cells?
why: Sulphonylureas close K-ATP channels, depolarising beta cells, and can cause hypoglycaemia (omit on the day of surgery). Metformin reduces hepatic glucose output; pioglitazone is a PPAR-γ agonist; SGLT2 inhibitors cause glycosuria; DPP-4 inhibitors increase incretins.

q: What is the equivalent dose of hydrocortisone to 5 mg of prednisolone in glucocorticoid potency?
why: Hydrocortisone 20 mg ≈ prednisolone 5 mg ≈ dexamethasone 0.75 mg in glucocorticoid potency. Dexamethasone has negligible mineralocorticoid activity; fludrocortisone is mainly mineralocorticoid.

sb: Effect of Drugs on the Eye
q: Which drug used in anaesthesia increases intraocular pressure?
why: Suxamethonium transiently raises IOP by about 5–10 mmHg (extraocular muscle tonic contraction and choroidal vasodilatation). Ketamine may increase it slightly. Most induction agents, volatiles and opioids lower IOP.

sb: Effect of Drugs on the Eye
q: Echothiophate eye drops used for glaucoma can prolong the action of which drug?
why: Echothiophate is a long-acting anticholinesterase that inhibits plasma cholinesterase, prolonging suxamethonium and mivacurium. Timolol drops can cause bradycardia and bronchospasm; acetazolamide causes metabolic acidosis and hypokalaemia.

q: Which volatile agent has the lowest blood:gas partition coefficient?
why: Blood:gas coefficients: desflurane 0.42, N2O 0.47, sevoflurane 0.65–0.69, isoflurane 1.4, halothane 2.4. Lower solubility means faster onset and offset.

q: Which volatile agent is most irritant to the airway and unsuitable for inhalational induction?
why: Desflurane (and isoflurane to a lesser extent) is pungent, causing coughing, breath-holding and laryngospasm, and can cause sympathetic stimulation with rapid increases in concentration. Sevoflurane is non-irritant and used for gas induction.

q: Which antibiotic class acts by inhibiting bacterial cell wall synthesis through binding penicillin-binding proteins?
why: Beta-lactams (penicillins, cephalosporins, carbapenems) bind PBPs, inhibiting peptidoglycan cross-linking. Glycopeptides (vancomycin) bind D-Ala-D-Ala. Aminoglycosides and macrolides inhibit protein synthesis; fluoroquinolones inhibit DNA gyrase.

q: Which antibiotic can prolong neuromuscular block by reducing acetylcholine release?
why: Aminoglycosides reduce presynaptic calcium entry and acetylcholine release, potentiating non-depolarising blockers. They are also nephrotoxic and ototoxic, so levels are monitored. Clindamycin and polymyxins can also potentiate block.

q: How does aciclovir work?
why: Aciclovir is selectively activated by herpesvirus thymidine kinase and then inhibits viral DNA polymerase (chain termination). Oseltamivir inhibits influenza neuraminidase. It can crystallise in the kidneys, so maintain hydration.

q: Which antifungal class acts by inhibiting synthesis of beta-1,3-glucan in the fungal cell wall?
why: Echinocandins (caspofungin, micafungin, anidulafungin) inhibit glucan synthesis. Azoles inhibit ergosterol synthesis (and CYP3A4 in humans); polyenes (amphotericin) bind ergosterol, forming pores, and are nephrotoxic.
